items.title: Good Governance — Concept & Attributes
items.body:
### Good governance

**In one line**
Good governance means running the country's affairs in a way that is citizen-centric, transparent and accountable — not just exercising power, but exercising it well.

**The story**
For decades 'governance' simply meant the government taking decisions. From the 1990s, the United Nations and the World Bank argued that *how* a government decides matters as much as *what* it decides. If citizens have no voice, if rules are applied unfairly, or if officials cannot be questioned, development stalls and corruption grows. So a checklist of qualities — the attributes of **good governance** — was drawn up to judge whether power is being used for the people. In India this became the reform slogan **'minimum government, maximum governance'**: fewer needless controls, better delivery.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
This is the umbrella concept for the whole topic — RTI, Citizen's Charter, social audit and e-governance are all tools that deliver one or more of these attributes. Prelims asks which items are, or are not, UN attributes; Mains asks you to use the attributes as a framework.

**Picture it — the eight UNESCAP attributes**

| # | Attribute | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Participation | Citizens have a voice in decisions |
| 2 | Rule of law | Fair laws, impartially enforced |
| 3 | Transparency | Information is freely available |
| 4 | Responsiveness | Institutions serve people in reasonable time |
| 5 | Consensus-oriented | Differing interests are mediated |
| 6 | Equity & inclusiveness | Everyone feels they have a stake |
| 7 | Effectiveness & efficiency | Best use of resources |
| 8 | Accountability | Government answers for its actions |

**Terms explained**
- **UNESCAP** — the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific, the body that listed these eight attributes.
- **Accountability** — being answerable; a citizen can ask an official 'why?' and expect a reply.
- **Rule of law** — the same law applies to everyone, including the government.

**Don't confuse**
- Good governance (how power is used) is wider than e-governance (using computers to deliver services) — e-governance is only one tool of good governance.
- 'Concentration of authority in the executive' is the OPPOSITE of good governance, not an attribute of it.

**Remember it**
Good governance disperses and checks power; dictatorship concentrates it. The four most-tested attributes are Participation, Rule of law, Transparency, Accountability.

**TL;DR**
- Good governance = citizen-centric, transparent, accountable administration.
- UNESCAP lists eight attributes (see the table).
- India's motto: 'minimum government, maximum governance'.
- Good Governance Day is 25 December (Vajpayee's birthday).
- Enablers: RTI, Citizen's Charter/Sevottam, social audit, e-governance.
keyPoints: Good governance = citizen-centric, transparent and accountable administration.
UNESCAP's eight attributes: participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, consensus-oriented, equity & inclusiveness, effectiveness & efficiency, accountability.
Indian reform motto: 'minimum government, maximum governance'.
Good Governance Day is 25 December (Vajpayee's birthday).
Key enablers: RTI, Citizen's Charter/Sevottam, social audit, e-governance.
items.mnemonic: Four core attributes to never forget: Participation, Rule of law, Transparency, Accountability.

items.title: Right to Information (RTI) Act 2005
items.body:
### Right to Information

**In one line**
The RTI Act 2005 gives every citizen the legal right to ask the government for information and get a reply within a fixed time — turning official secrecy into openness.

**The story**
Before 2005, officials could refuse information citing colonial-era secrecy. A grassroots movement (notably the MKSS in Rajasthan, demanding to see wage records) argued that the **right to know** flows from the **right to free speech** in Article 19(1)(a) — you cannot speak meaningfully about public affairs if the facts are hidden. Parliament enacted the RTI Act (passed 15 June 2005; in force **12 October 2005**), replacing the weaker, never-enforced Freedom of Information Act 2002. Each public office now has an officer who must answer requests, and refusals can be appealed.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
RTI is the single biggest transparency tool and a favourite exam topic — the appeal ladder, the 30-day limit, Sections 4 and 8, and the 2019 amendment are all tested.

**Picture it — how a request moves**

| Stage | Who | Time limit |
|---|---|---|
| Request | Public Information Officer (PIO) | 30 days (48 hours if life/liberty) |
| First appeal | First Appellate Authority (a senior officer) | 30 days |
| Second appeal | Information Commission (CIC / State IC) | final |

**Terms explained**
- **PIO (Public Information Officer)** — the designated officer in each public body who receives and answers RTI requests.
- **FAA (First Appellate Authority)** — a senior officer in the same body who hears the first appeal.
- **Information Commission** — the independent final authority (central CIC, state SICs) that can order disclosure and fine a PIO.
- **Section 4** — proactive (suo motu) disclosure: offices must publish key information on their own, so fewer people need to file requests.
- **Section 8** — the list of exempt information (national security, cabinet papers, personal data with no public purpose), but even this can be released when the larger public interest outweighs the harm (Section 8(2)).

**Don't confuse**
- RTI is a **statutory** right (made by Parliament), not a Fundamental Right — though it flows from the Fundamental Right in Article 19(1)(a).
- First appeal goes to the FAA, NOT straight to the Information Commission or a court.

**Remember it**
'PIO → FAA → Commission' — the ladder always climbs upward; 30 days at each citizen step, 48 hours only when life or liberty is at stake.

**TL;DR**
- RTI Act in force 12 October 2005; flows from Article 19(1)(a).
- PIO must reply in 30 days (48 hours for life/liberty).
- Appeal ladder: PIO → First Appellate Authority → Information Commission.
- Section 4 = proactive disclosure; Section 8 = exemptions with a public-interest override.
- The 2019 amendment moved Commissioners' tenure/salary to Central Government rules.
keyPoints: RTI Act enacted 2005; came into force 12 October 2005; flows from Article 19(1)(a).
PIO must respond in 30 days (48 hours where life/liberty is involved).
Appeal ladder: PIO → First Appellate Authority → Information Commission (CIC/SIC).
Section 4 = proactive disclosure; Section 8 = exemptions with a larger-public-interest override.
RTI (Amendment) Act 2019 moved tenure/salary of Information Commissioners to Central Government rules.
items.mnemonic: 30 days for the PIO, 30 days for the first appeal, 48 hours for life & liberty.
items.source: RTI Act 2005 & RTI (Amendment) Act 2019, India Code (rti.gov.in)

items.title: Citizen's Charter & the Sevottam Model
items.body:
### Citizen's Charter and Sevottam

**In one line**
A Citizen's Charter is a public promise by an office about what service you will get and by when; Sevottam is the DARPG framework that checks whether offices actually keep that promise.

**The story**
Citizens often did not know what service they were entitled to, or whom to complain to when it failed. The United Kingdom answered this in **1991** (under PM John Major) with the **Citizen's Charter** idea: publish your service standards openly. India liked it and adopted it at the **1997 Conference of Chief Ministers**. But a charter is only a promise, so DARPG built **Sevottam** ('Seva' + 'Uttam' = excellence in service) to assess and improve delivery across three linked modules. Where promises had to become enforceable, states passed **Public Service Guarantee laws** — Madhya Pradesh first in 2010.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
Exam questions test the UK origin (1991) and India adoption (1997), the fact that a charter is voluntary and non-justiciable, the three Sevottam modules, and which state passed the first service-guarantee law.

**Picture it — the three Sevottam modules**

| Module | Focus |
|---|---|
| 1. Citizen's Charter | Publish service standards |
| 2. Public grievance redress | Handle and resolve complaints |
| 3. Service delivery capability | Strengthen the office to deliver |

**Terms explained**
- **Non-justiciable** — you cannot sue in court merely because a charter promise was broken; it is a moral commitment, not a contract.
- **DARPG** — Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances, the nodal department for these reforms.
- **Public Service Guarantee law** — a state law that fixes service timelines and penalises officials who delay, turning the charter promise into an enforceable right.
- **Six UK charter principles** — quality, choice, standards, value, accountability, transparency.

**Don't confuse**
- A Citizen's Charter (voluntary promise) is NOT the same as a Public Service Guarantee Act (enforceable, penalty-backed).
- Sevottam is an Indian (DARPG) framework; the Citizen's Charter idea itself began in the UK.

**Remember it**
Sevottam = three C's — Charter, Complaints (redress), Capability. The charter promises; the guarantee law enforces.

**TL;DR**
- Citizen's Charter originated in the UK (1991); India adopted it in 1997; it is voluntary and non-justiciable.
- Six principles: quality, choice, standards, value, accountability, transparency.
- Sevottam's three modules: Charter, grievance redress, service-delivery capability.
- Public Service Guarantee laws make standards time-bound with penalties.
- Madhya Pradesh enacted India's first such law (2010).
keyPoints: Citizen's Charter originated in the UK (1991); India adopted it in 1997; it is voluntary/non-justiciable.
Six charter principles: quality, choice, standards, value, accountability, transparency.
Sevottam = Seva + Uttam; three modules: Citizen's Charter, grievance redress, service-delivery capability (DARPG).
Public Service Delivery Guarantee laws make service standards time-bound with penalties.
Madhya Pradesh enacted India's first Public Service Guarantee Act (2010).
items.mnemonic: Sevottam = 'Seva Uttam' → 3 C's: Charter, Complaints (redress), Capability.
items.source: DARPG Citizen's Charter & Sevottam guidelines (darpg.gov.in); MP Public Service Guarantee Act 2010

items.title: Social Audit & Accountability
items.body:
### Social audit

**In one line**
A social audit is a public meeting where ordinary citizens and beneficiaries check the government's own records against the work actually done on the ground.

**The story**
Official records can say a road was built or wages were paid when nothing happened. The remedy is to read those records aloud in front of the village — the people who were supposed to benefit will spot the fake entries at once. **MGNREGA (2005), Section 17** made this a legal duty: the **Gram Sabha** must regularly audit all works under the scheme. This was India's first large statutory social-audit mandate, and it was later extended in principle to other schemes and to dedicated social-audit units in the states.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
Social audit is the headline accountability tool, and Andhra Pradesh is its national model — a very common AP-angle exam point. Questions test the MGNREGA Section 17 mandate and the role of SSAAT.

**Picture it — who does what**

| Element | Role |
|---|---|
| Gram Sabha | Hears records read out, questions them |
| Social-audit unit (SSAAT in AP) | Independent team that gathers and verifies records |
| Records checked | Muster rolls, bills, lists of works |

**Terms explained**
- **Gram Sabha** — the assembly of all adult voters of a village; the forum where the audit happens.
- **Muster roll** — the official attendance-and-wage register for workers on a public work.
- **SSAAT** — the Society for Social Audit, Accountability and Transparency, Andhra Pradesh's independent, arm's-length social-audit body.

**Don't confuse**
- Social audit is done by an independent unit WITH the Gram Sabha — NOT directly by the CAG (though the CAG has issued social-audit standards).
- Social audit (citizens verify) is different from a financial audit (accountants check books).

**Remember it**
'Read the records to the village' — that one image is the whole idea. AP's SSAAT made it a permanent institution.

**TL;DR**
- Social audit = citizens/Gram Sabha verify official records against actual work.
- MGNREGA 2005, Section 17 makes it a statutory Gram Sabha duty.
- It is a key accountability and anti-corruption tool.
- Andhra Pradesh pioneered institutionalised social audit via SSAAT.
- The AP model informed national social-audit standards and state units.
keyPoints: Social audit = citizens/Gram Sabha verify official records against actual work on the ground.
MGNREGA 2005, Section 17 makes social audit by the Gram Sabha a statutory mandate.
It is a key accountability and anti-corruption tool in public expenditure.
Andhra Pradesh pioneered institutionalised social audits via SSAAT.
The AP model informed national social-audit standards and state social-audit units.
items.mnemonic: Social audit = 'read the records to the village'; AP's SSAAT made it permanent.

items.title: e-Governance — Types, NeGP & Digital India
items.body:
### e-Governance

**In one line**
e-Governance means using computers, the internet and mobile phones to deliver government services so that they are faster, cheaper, more transparent and reach the citizen's doorstep.

**The story**
Standing in long queues and paying bribes to a clerk was the old way of getting a certificate. From the 2000s the government began putting services online. The **National e-Governance Plan (NeGP), approved in 2006**, organised this effort around **Mission Mode Projects** and aimed to deliver services through common outlets near where people live. Its upgraded version, **e-Kranti (NeGP 2.0)**, became a **pillar of Digital India (launched 1 July 2015)**. Services are grouped by who talks to whom — the four 'G2' interaction types.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
The four interaction types, the NeGP-to-Digital-India sequence, and the main platforms are standard Prelims matter; AP's delivery stack is the AP angle.

**Picture it — the four interaction types**

| Type | Interaction | Example |
|---|---|---|
| G2C | Government to Citizen | Online certificates, pensions |
| G2B | Government to Business | MCA21 corporate filings, licences |
| G2G | Government to Government | Inter-agency data sharing |
| G2E | Government to Employee | Payroll, leave portals |

**Terms explained**
- **Mission Mode Project (MMP)** — a focused e-governance project (such as land records or passports) run like a time-bound mission.
- **e-Kranti** — NeGP 2.0, with the motto 'Transforming e-Governance for Transforming Governance'.
- **CPGRAMS** — the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System, the online portal to lodge and track complaints.
- **G2C / G2B / G2G / G2E** — Government-to-Citizen / Business / Government / Employee.

**Don't confuse**
- NeGP (2006) is the plan; Digital India (2015) is the later umbrella programme; e-Kranti is the bridge between them.
- MCA21 (filing company returns) is G2B, not G2C — the user is a business, not a citizen.

**Remember it**
All four relationships start with 'G2' and end in C, B, G, E — Citizen, Business, Government, Employee.

**TL;DR**
- e-Governance uses ICT for faster, transparent service delivery.
- Interaction types: G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E.
- NeGP (2006) built around Mission Mode Projects → e-Kranti (NeGP 2.0) → Digital India (1 July 2015).
- CPGRAMS is the centralised online grievance portal.
- The technology side (cyber security, DPDP Act) sits under Science-Tech.
keyPoints: e-Governance interaction types: G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E.
NeGP was approved in 2006 and built around Mission Mode Projects (MMPs).
e-Kranti (NeGP 2.0) is a pillar of Digital India — 'Transforming e-Governance for Transforming Governance'.
Digital India was launched on 1 July 2015 as the umbrella programme.
CPGRAMS (DARPG) is the centralised online public-grievance portal.
items.mnemonic: Four e-gov relationships all start with 'G2' → C, B, G, E (Citizen, Business, Government, Employee).
items.source: MeitY — NeGP / e-Kranti / Digital India (meity.gov.in); DARPG CPGRAMS

items.title: 2nd ARC & Andhra Pradesh's Governance Model
items.body:
### The 2nd ARC and Andhra Pradesh's model

**In one line**
The Second Administrative Reforms Commission was an expert body that wrote the blueprint for governance reform in India, and Andhra Pradesh is the state that has put many of those ideas into practice.

**The story**
In **2005** the government set up the **Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2nd ARC)**, first chaired by **M. Veerappa Moily** (later V. Ramachandran). Over **15 reports** it recommended how to make administration honest, citizen-friendly and tech-enabled — its very first report called RTI the 'Master Key to Good Governance'. Andhra Pradesh then became a showcase for citizen-service delivery, building real-time monitoring, single-window and even WhatsApp-based services.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
The 2nd ARC's report titles and the SMART formula are directly tested; AP's RTGS, MeeSeva and Mana Mitra are the state-angle favourites.

**Picture it — key 2nd ARC reports and AP initiatives**

| 2nd ARC report | Theme |
|---|---|
| 1st — 'RTI: Master Key to Good Governance' | Transparency |
| 4th — 'Ethics in Governance' | Integrity |
| 11th — 'Promoting e-Governance: The SMART Way Forward' | e-governance |
| 12th — 'Citizen Centric Administration' | Service delivery |

| AP initiative | What it does |
|---|---|
| RTGS (Real Time Governance Society) | Real-time monitoring and grievance command centre |
| MeeSeva ('at your service') | Single-window certificate and G2C delivery |
| Mana Mitra | Delivers government services via WhatsApp |
| e-Pragati | State enterprise-architecture integrating departments |

**Terms explained**
- **SMART governance** — Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent (the 2nd ARC's e-governance ideal).
- **Enterprise architecture** — a common technical design that lets different departments share data and talk to each other (e-Pragati).
- **RTGS (here)** — Andhra Pradesh's Real Time Governance Society, NOT the banking money-transfer system of the same abbreviation.

**Don't confuse**
- The 2nd ARC (2005, Moily) is different from the 1st ARC (1966, chaired first by Morarji Desai, then K. Hanumanthaiah).
- AP's 'RTGS' is a governance body; the RTGS you know from banking is unrelated.

**Remember it**
SMART = Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent — the five letters capture the 2nd ARC's whole e-governance vision.

**TL;DR**
- 2nd ARC (2005) was first chaired by Veerappa Moily and gave 15 reports.
- 1st report: 'RTI — Master Key'; 12th: 'Citizen Centric Administration'.
- SMART governance = Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent.
- AP RTGS runs a real-time monitoring and grievance command centre.
- AP MeeSeva = single-window delivery; Mana Mitra delivers via WhatsApp.
keyPoints: 2nd ARC (2005) was first chaired by Veerappa Moily and submitted 15 reports.
1st report: 'RTI — Master Key to Good Governance'; 12th: 'Citizen Centric Administration'.
SMART governance = Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent (11th report on e-Governance).
AP RTGS runs an integrated real-time monitoring and grievance command-and-control centre.
AP MeeSeva = single-window G2C service delivery; Mana Mitra delivers services via WhatsApp.
items.mnemonic: SMART = Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent — the 2nd ARC's e-governance ideal.
items.source: Second ARC reports (arc.gov.in); AP Real Time Governance Society (rtgs.ap.gov.in)

items.title: Development processes — civil society, NGOs, SHGs, pressure groups & stakeholders
items.body:
### Actors in the development process

**In one line**
Development today is not done by government alone — civil society, NGOs, self-help groups and pressure groups all take part as stakeholders, each playing a role the state cannot play by itself.

**The story**
For a long time 'development' meant schemes handed down by officials. Experience showed that programmes work better when the people they are meant to help are organised and involved — they reach the last mile, spot leakages, and demand accountability. So the development process opened up to many **stakeholders**: voluntary associations (**civil society**), organised non-profits (**NGOs**), village savings groups (**SHGs**), and interest groups that lobby for policy (**pressure groups**). Andhra Pradesh built one of India's densest networks of women's self-help groups to deliver anti-poverty programmes.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
This feeds the Mains clause on development processes and is tested in Prelims through definitions and the AP SHG bodies (DWCRA, SERP, MEPMA).

**Picture it — the Andhra Pradesh SHG bodies**

| Body | Role |
|---|---|
| DWCRA | Development of Women and Children in Rural Areas — early (1982-83) women's SHG scheme |
| SERP | Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty — runs Velugu / Indira Kranthi Patham |
| MEPMA | Mission for Elimination of Poverty in Municipal Areas — urban SHG arm |
| DAY-NRLM | National Rural Livelihoods Mission that AP's SHGs feed into |

**Terms explained**
- **Civil society** — the space of voluntary, non-state, non-market associations (community groups, unions, welfare bodies) that mobilise citizens and hold the state to account.
- **NGO (non-governmental organisation)** — an organised non-profit body delivering services, advocacy and awareness.
- **Self-Help Group (SHG)** — a small (usually 10-20) voluntary group, mostly of women, that pools savings and accesses bank credit.
- **Pressure group** — an organised interest (union, farmer or business body) that influences policy without contesting elections.
- **Stakeholder** — anyone who affects or is affected by a programme.

**Don't confuse**
- A pressure group influences policy but does NOT seek office; a political party contests elections to form government.
- An NGO is a formal organisation; 'civil society' is the broader space that includes NGOs, unions and informal groups.

**Remember it**
SHGs climb a ladder — SHG → Village Organisation → Mandal Samakhya — and feed into DAY-NRLM.

**TL;DR**
- Development involves many stakeholders: civil society, NGOs, SHGs, pressure groups, PRIs, private sector, government.
- Civil society mobilises citizens and holds the state accountable.
- An SHG is a small (10-20) voluntary savings-and-credit group, mostly of women.
- A pressure group influences policy without contesting elections.
- AP: DWCRA (1982-83) seeded the movement; SERP runs Velugu/IKP; MEPMA is the urban arm.
keyPoints: Development involves many stakeholders: civil society, NGOs, SHGs, pressure groups, PRIs, private sector, government.
Civil society = voluntary non-state, non-market associations that hold the state accountable.
A Self-Help Group (SHG) is a small (10-20) voluntary savings-and-credit group, mostly of women.
A pressure group (union, farmer/business body) influences policy without contesting elections.

SHG federation ladder: SHG → Village Organisation → Mandal Samakhya; feeds DAY-NRLM.

items.title: PYQ Precision — Aadhaar, Aspirational Districts & Platforms
items.body:
### Aadhaar, Aspirational Districts and e-gov platforms

**In one line**
Three high-frequency exam facts: how the Aadhaar Act was passed, what the Aspirational Districts Programme does, and which platform does what.

**The story**
The government uses Aadhaar to send subsidies straight to a beneficiary's bank account (Direct Benefit Transfer), cutting out middlemen. To pass the enabling law quickly, the **Aadhaar Act 2016** was certified as a **Money Bill** — a route the Supreme Court later upheld (majority) while striking down Section 57. To lift the most backward districts, **NITI Aayog** launched the **Aspirational Districts Programme (2018)**, ranking districts so they compete to improve. A family of digital platforms now delivers services and takes complaints.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
These are repeat Prelims facts (including a UPSC 2017 item on Aadhaar) and need to be remembered precisely.

**Picture it — the main platforms**

| Platform | Function |
|---|---|
| UMANG | Unified mobile app for government services |
| DigiLocker | Digital document storage |
| MyGov | Citizen engagement and participation |
| CPGRAMS | Public grievance redress |
| CSCs | Last-mile delivery outlets |

**Terms explained**
- **Money Bill** — a bill dealing only with taxes or spending from the Consolidated Fund; the Speaker certifies it, and the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes (Article 110).
- **DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer)** — paying a subsidy directly into the beneficiary's account.
- **Consolidated Fund of India** — the main government account into which revenues flow and from which authorised spending is drawn.
- **Aspirational Districts five themes** — health & nutrition, education, agriculture & water, financial inclusion & skilling, basic infrastructure.

**Don't confuse**
- UMANG (one app for many services) is not DigiLocker (document storage) — a common mismatch in match-the-following questions.
- The Aspirational Districts Programme (2018) was later extended as the Aspirational Blocks Programme (2023); do not merge the two years.

**Remember it**
Aspirational Districts run on the three C's — Convergence, Collaboration, Competition.

**TL;DR**
- Aadhaar Act 2016 was passed as a Money Bill; enables targeted DBT; Section 57 struck down (2018).
- Aspirational Districts Programme (2018) is anchored by NITI Aayog with five themes.
- UMANG = unified app; DigiLocker = document storage; MyGov = citizen engagement.
- CPGRAMS = grievance redress; CSCs = last-mile outlets, all under Digital India.
- Aspirational Districts motto: Convergence, Collaboration, Competition.
keyPoints: Aadhaar Act 2016 was passed as a Money Bill; enables targeted DBT of subsidies; Section 57 struck down (2018).
Aspirational Districts Programme (2018) is anchored by NITI Aayog with five themes.
UMANG = unified mobile app; DigiLocker = document storage; MyGov = citizen engagement.
CPGRAMS = grievance redress; CSCs = last-mile delivery, all under Digital India.
Aspirational Districts motto: Convergence, Collaboration, Competition.
items.source: UPSC 2017 Prelims; Aadhaar Act 2016; NITI Aayog; MeitY/DARPG

items.title: MPLADS, Department of Personnel & Urban Bodies
items.body:
### MPLADS, Department of Personnel and urban bodies

**In one line**
Three smaller but tested facts: how the MP local-area development fund works, when the Department of Personnel was created, and two urban-governance bodies.

**The story**
Each Member of Parliament can recommend local works (such as a school building or a borewell) under the **MPLAD Scheme**; the money does not lapse at year-end, so it can be carried forward, and a share is reserved for SC/ST areas with a minimum inspection norm to curb misuse. Separately, India needed a professional civil-service-reform agency, so after the **N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar Committee** the **Department of Personnel** was set up in **1970 under the Prime Minister** (later the DoPT). On the urban side, two bodies recur in questions.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
These appear as 'consider the statements' Prelims items; the precise facts (non-lapsable, 10% inspection, 1970/PM, apex body) are what gets tested.

**Picture it — the three facts**

| Item | Key fact |
|---|---|
| MPLADS | Non-lapsable funds; durable assets; SC/ST earmarking; at least 10% of works inspected |
| Department of Personnel | Set up 1970 under the Prime Minister (after Ayyangar Committee) |
| NIUA | Apex body of the Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs |
| India Sanitation Coalition | Platform that mobilises funding for sustainable sanitation |

**Terms explained**
- **MPLADS** — Members of Parliament Local Area Development Scheme.
- **Non-lapsable** — unspent money is carried forward to the next year instead of being surrendered.
- **NIUA** — National Institute of Urban Affairs, the apex urban-affairs body of the Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs.
- **India Sanitation Coalition** — a private-sector-led platform mobilising funds for sustainable sanitation (NOT a Government-plus-WHO body).

**Don't confuse**
- The India Sanitation Coalition is an industry-led platform, not a government + WHO body.
- The Department of Personnel was under the Prime Minister, not the Finance Ministry or the UPSC.

**Remember it**
MPLADS = money that does not die at year-end; '1970 + PM' fixes the Department of Personnel.

**TL;DR**
- MPLADS funds are non-lapsable, for durable assets, with SC/ST earmarking and 10% district inspection.
- The Department of Personnel was set up in 1970 under the PM after the N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar Committee.
- NIUA is the apex body of the Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs.
- The India Sanitation Coalition mobilises funding for sustainable sanitation.
keyPoints: MPLADS funds are non-lapsable, for durable assets, with SC/ST earmarking and 10% district inspection.
The Department of Personnel was set up in 1970 under the PM; the N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar Committee had urged reform.
NIUA is the apex body of the Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs; the India Sanitation Coalition mobilises sanitation funding.

items.title: For Mains — Governance, Transparency & e-Governance
items.body:
## For Mains — the analytical frame

Mains (Paper-III, clauses M3-8 development processes and M3-10 good governance & e-governance) does not reward listing facts; it rewards a **framework** — tools of good governance assessed on what they achieve, where they fall short, and how to fix them.

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Concept | Good governance = participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, accountability (UNESCAP); 'minimum government, maximum governance' |
| Instruments | Transparency → RTI, Section 4 proactive disclosure; Accountability → social audit (MGNREGA Sec 17); Responsiveness → Citizen's Charter, Sevottam, CPGRAMS; Efficiency/access → e-governance (NeGP, Digital India) |
| Significance | Reduces corruption, empowers citizens, improves last-mile delivery, deepens democracy between elections |
| Criticism / limits | RTI pendency and the 2019 dilution of Commissioners' independence; charters non-justiciable; digital divide; exclusion errors in Aadhaar-linked delivery; uneven social-audit quality |
| Way forward | Autonomous, well-staffed Information Commissions; statutory protection for RTI activists and social auditors; inclusive, multi-channel (assisted/offline) e-governance; integrate service platforms with grievance redress |

**Data points / reports / schemes to quote**
- 2nd ARC — 1st report 'RTI: Master Key to Good Governance'; 11th 'Promoting e-Governance: SMART Way'; 12th 'Citizen Centric Administration'.
- RTI Act 2005 (Art 19(1)(a)); RTI (Amendment) Act 2019.
- MGNREGA 2005, Section 17 (social audit).
- Digital India (1 July 2015); e-Kranti; CPGRAMS; UMANG/DigiLocker.
- MP Public Service Guarantee Act 2010 (first such law).

**AP angle**
Andhra Pradesh is a ready case study: SSAAT (institutionalised social audit), RTGS (real-time command-and-control centre), MeeSeva (single-window), Mana Mitra (WhatsApp governance), and women's SHG federations under SERP/Velugu — a complete transparency-plus-delivery stack.

**Use in answers**
- Open with the UNESCAP attributes as a yardstick, then map each tool to an attribute.
- Quote the 2nd ARC's 'Master Key' line for RTI.
- Diagram idea: a simple pyramid — Transparency (RTI) + Accountability (social audit) as the base, Responsiveness (charter) and Efficiency (e-gov) as the next tier, Good Governance at the apex.
- Always close with a balanced way-forward paragraph (independence + inclusion).
